title: Zero, Negative Numbers, and Order on the Number Line

blocks.text: A Reference Point and Two Directions

When counting counters, natural numbers are usually enough. Other situations require us to express which side of a reference point we are on. A temperature may be below zero; a level may be below a chosen surface. Integers include the natural numbers and their opposites: negative numbers, zero, and positive numbers. The sign is part of the number and changes its meaning.

To represent them on a number line, we choose zero as the origin and a constant spacing as the unit. Positive numbers are placed to the right; negative numbers to the left. There is one unit between two consecutive integer marks. If the origin represents a surface, a negative value indicates a position below it; it does not mean that a negative length exists.

Zero is neither positive nor negative. It marks the reference point from which we measure position. A person standing at the origin is at a distance of zero from that origin. In a physical context, you must know what was chosen as the reference point: changing the reference may change the numerical values of positions without moving the objects.

On the number line, the number farther to the right is greater. That is why \(-2>-7\): minus two is to the right of minus seven. Comparing only 2 with 7 and copying that comparison ignores the meaning of the sign. On a temperature scale, two degrees below zero is warmer than seven degrees below zero.

The symbols \(<\) and \(>\) compare values. The open side faces the greater value: \(-7<-2\). A comparison can be written either way without changing its meaning. Every negative number is less than zero; every positive number is greater. Before comparing, locate both numbers relative to zero, then check their positions.

The distance from zero measures how many units separate a position from the origin. It is a nonnegative quantity: both -5 and 5 are five units away from zero. Distance and position answer different questions. If all you know is that someone is five meters from the origin, you still need to know which of the two directions they are in.
The Opposite Is Not Always Negative

Two opposite numbers are the same distance from zero, on opposite sides. The opposite of 4 is -4; the opposite of -4 is 4; and the opposite of 0 is 0. If we use the letter \(a\) to represent an integer, we write its opposite as \(-a\). The letter may stand for a positive number, a negative number, or zero. The sign in front indicates the operation of taking the opposite.

For example, if \(a=-6\), then \(-a=-(-6)=6\). Taking the opposite twice returns the original number. This rule is not limited to negative numbers: \(-(-3)=3\) as well, and the opposite of zero taken twice is zero. The number line explains this operation as a reflection across the origin.

To read an unlabeled mark, first find zero and observe the interval between the marks. Do not start counting from the edge of the image as though the values necessarily began there. A drawn interval represents the indicated unit, not a physical length on the screen.
We will use the distance from zero in a concrete sense. A position can be negative; its distance from the origin never is.

blocks.prompt: The marks on the number line are one unit apart. Which integer does the point indicate?

feedback.correct: The mark is four units to the left of zero: it represents -4.
feedback.incorrect: The distance is 4, but the question asks for the position. Being to the left of zero requires a negative sign.

blocks.prompt: The point on the number line represents a position. Enter that position and its distance from zero.

feedback.correct: The position is -6 and the distance is 6 units. The sign expresses direction, not a negative distance.
feedback.incorrect: Do not enter -6 as the distance. Check what each field asks for: location relative to the origin and separation from the origin.

blocks.prompt: Arrange the numbers from smallest to largest.

feedback.correct: From left to right on the number line: -8 < -3 < 0 < 2 < 7.
feedback.incorrect: Among negative numbers, the one farther from zero lies farther to the left. Do not order the digits while ignoring their signs.

blocks.text: Opposites and a New Reference Point

blocks.prompt: Match each integer with its opposite.

feedback.correct: The pairs are -9 and 9; 4 and -4; zero and zero.
feedback.incorrect: The opposite changes sides without changing the distance. Zero stays at the origin and is its own opposite.

blocks.prompt: The letter a represents -5. Which statement is correct?

options.label: -a equals -5 because it is always negative.
-a equals 5 because it is the opposite of -5.

feedback.correct: The opposite of -5 is 5. The sign of -a depends on the value of a.
feedback.incorrect: The first option confuses the written minus sign with the sign of the result. Taking the opposite does not give zero: it places the number at the same distance on the other side.

blocks.prompt: A mark is 3 m below a surface that we take as zero. Which integer expresses its position?

feedback.correct: The position is -3 m relative to the surface. The distance to the surface is 3 m.
feedback.incorrect: Below the surface corresponds to the negative side of the reference point. A positive value would indicate above it.
